analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "The case is submitted. We'll hear arguments at 1 o'clock in Penhurst against Haldeman. Mr. Farr, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. May it please the Court. This case, as it now stands before this Court, is essentially a dispute between citizens of the State of Pennsylvania and the State itself over how to run the State Mental Retardation Program pursuant to State law. The Federal Court saw fit to decide this dispute, imposing upon the State a mandatory presumption in favor of certain types of programs and requiring the State to create and pay for new facilities in accordance with its preference. In our view, this Federal interference in purely State matters is barred by the 11th Amendment and by principles of comedy. Now, this afternoon, I will discuss the 11th Amendment and Alan Warshaw will discuss the issue of comedy. Before getting into the details of our 11th Amendment argument, I think it might be useful to the Court if we state as straightforwardly as possible just what our overall position is. In short, we believe, first, that this claim is in fact a claim against the State and not just against State officials. Second, that the State is not prevented from claiming its 11th Amendment immunity by the doctrine of ex parte young, which by its terms and logic applies only to Federal claims. And third, that the State may invoke its immunity against a pending claim, just as it may invoke its immunity against primary claims. Now, as the statement of the State and the State of the State, proper 11th Amendment analysis requires the asking of several separate, though related, questions. Is it a claim against the State? Is it within the doctrine of ex parte young? And is the 11th Amendment somehow inapplicable to pending claims? In addressing the first of these questions, whether the claim is in fact one against the State, it is not dispositive that the complaint only names State officials as defendants. This Court has said on numerous occasions that the courts must look to the nature of the claim and the nature of the relief sought to determine whether it is in effect one against the State. Now, there's no bright line to define this inquiry, but the basic test derived from Larson in 1949, a Federal case, but followed in subsequent cases, is whether the State officials can make a non-frivolous claim that they are acting, even if mistakenly, within the general ambit of their colorable authority under State law. Well, Mr. Farr, you refer to Larson as being a Federal case, but the plurality, at any rate, in treasurer's self, or has pretty much adopted that as an 11th Amendment rule, too. That's correct, yes, sir. Now, in this case, despite all of respondents' allegations about lawless behavior, we think it controlling that defendants are the persons charged by state law with making the numerous, almost day-to-day discretionary decisions about operation of the state mental retardation program, including the very decisions that are at issue in this case. What kind of facilities to create? What kinds of persons to put in those kinds of facilities? What kinds of services and programs to provide? Furthermore, it is clear that these defendants must make those decisions within the limits of the funding provided by the state legislature. Respondents simply want them to make different decisions and to exact from the state treasury the money to pay for those decisions. But under the test set down by this court, that is the very essence of a suit against the state itself. Now, the second question is whether even though the claim is functionally won against the state itself, it is within the venerable doctrine of ex parte young. For if the claim were that the state officials were violating the federal constitution or federal law, then ex parte young says that the state cannot give them its immunity from the 11th Amendment. They are required to be obedient to the superior authority of federal law. But young has never been thought to apply to state law claims like the ones here, nor should it be. The practical need for the so-called fiction of ex parte young, that the state officials are stripped of their representative character, is necessary to be able to enforce the 14th Amendment and other federal laws in the language of this court in Edelman to turn the civil rights amendments from a shield into a sword. But that need is not present when you are dealing with only a state law claim. In fact, the proper balance between the local and the national governments is much better preserved with important state issues by having those questions decided by a state court. Mr. Parr, let me just be sure I understand one point. You do agree if it were a federal statutory claim, then you would say that would be covered by ex parte young? I do. Yes, I do. The third inquiry, and one by its terms which is an odd one to be asking at all, is whether the 11th Amendment is somehow inapplicable to pendant claims. Although some early cases conceitedly seem to incline in that direction, without, we think, very much consideration of the issue, we think that the decision in Edelman v. Jordan settled and settled correctly, that issue for once and for all. Let me see if I understand your response to Justice Stevens. Suppose the complaint asserts a federal question. Does that end the matter? As far as that particular claim goes, the court would have to, of course, see whether it had Article III jurisdiction over it. But if it seeks injunctive relief under a federal claim, that is permitted by ex parte young. You mean a federal statutory claim that would preclude the official doing what he's doing? That's correct. For example, in Ray... There was preemption, for example. Ray v. Atlantic Richfield is the example I was going to give, where the court said that the state officials, by carrying out the state law in that case, were preempted by federal law and were willing to give an injunction against the carrying out of state law. Now, that does not extend to retroactive belief. But other than that, the federal claims are within ex parte young. Turning back to Edelman and the question of pendant claims, in Edelman, the situation was that there was a primary claim, which was an equal protection claim under the 14th Amendment, a claim which in and of itself would be permitted by ex parte young. There were, in effect, two pendant claims under federal law. The court examined each of these claims, determined that one claim was permitted because it was under federal law and sought injunctive relief, as I was saying to the Chief Justice, and decided that the other claim was barred by the 11th Amendment because it was a federal claim but sought retroactive relief. The same analysis applies here. This pendant claim is barred by the 11th Amendment, not because it seeks retroactive relief, but because it is a state claim to which ex parte young does not apply at all. Well, that would help if you let us know what you are calling a state claim. The kind of a state claim you are talking about, I take it, is a claim that the official is acting outside the scope of his authority. That's correct. Just in terms of state law, he shouldn't be doing what he is doing. That's correct. And you can see that if there was an allegation, would you, or would you, that he's acting completely outside the... He has no even, no colorable authority under state law. Would the 11th Amendment still... In that situation, if you were, if the allegation was that he was so outside of his authority that he effectively was acting without any authority at all, then I think it would not be a claim against the state. I mean, we don't have to decide. I guess we don't have to decide that. In this case, nobody's claiming. They're just claiming that the state officials were misapplying state law. Well, I think, you know, I think if they get up on their feet, they'll claim that it's lawless and horrible and all of that. But I think basically the claim is that they are simply not making the right decisions under state law. Misconstruing state law. That's correct. What you're saying is you can't convert a dispute over the applicability of the state law into a claim of, quote, lawlessness, closed border, totally without authority. Absolutely. I think what you have to look at is whether the defendants can make a non-frivolous defense that they're acting within state law. I think once you've got that, then the inquiry stops. Otherwise, you're going to have a situation where the 11th Amendment means something only if you actually go through and decide the merits of the state law claim, which is not much to know. So, rationally, should you be able, for 11th Amendment purposes, to distinguish between some official who's acting totally outside of his authority and some official who's just misconstruing state law? Well, I think there is. And maybe Larson did, but does it make a whole lot of sense? Well, I think there are two points about that, Mr. Justice White. One is that I think that it makes sense only at the very outer boundary, which is that the mere fact that somebody happens to be employed by the state, of course, doesn't mean he can go around and do whatever he wants and then claim an 11th Amendment immunity in federal court. Well, why shouldn't the rationale of, as you say, the rationale of ex-parti young shouldn't reach that either? Well, I think you don't need the rationale. It shouldn't reach any state claim. Well, I think you don't need the rationale. What I'm saying is that there are points at which the behavior is so far outside the boundary that it really is just personal behavior, that someone is committing an assault on his own time. Why do you conclude from that that the 11th Amendment doesn't buy the suit? Well, because then I would say that there's really no state involvement at all, that if somebody is just acting on his individual, if somebody is driving his car for pleasure or something and he's sued in a diversity suit, that might be a situation where he just can't say, well, because I incidentally happen to have a job some of the rest of the time with a state, I'm covered by the 11th Amendment. But I think it's a very, very narrow limitation, and particularly because Larson, of course, is a federal case. In Larson, the situation is if you don't give some leeway for allowing those kinds of suits, they are effectively barred completely by sovereign immunity. But in the context of a claim against a state official, the only question we're addressing here is whether these claims can be brought in federal court. They can still be brought in state court, and therefore there's an alternative way to get those cases resolved. Mr. Farr, supposing a Pennsylvania statute said in so many words, none of these people shall be institutionalized in Pennhurst, would the 11th Amendment be a claim against someone who says, I'm being wrongfully institutionalized in Pennhurst? I think there is a level at which the statutes or the state law might be so absolutely clear that all the state officials had, they effectively had no discretion, there was simply a ministerial carrying out. I think under the cases of this court, that sort of case might be allowed in. What's your answer to my specific case? Whether that case is clear enough. If there's a claim, if they say absolutely no people are to be... The statute says no one shall be placed in Pennhurst. And the state appropriates no money to support Pennhurst, and they just do it on their own. No, they still pay the bills at Pennhurst. They do exactly what they're doing now, but the statute says no one shall be institutionalized in Pennhurst during 1983, you see. Well, the reason that I raise the funding is that if you're saying that nobody should be admitted to Pennhurst and there's a flat prohibition, I would think under the cases of this court, that that non-discretionary matter might be within the Treasurer-Salver's notion that somebody is proceeding outside the scope. So then the question, I gather, the way you present the argument, is whether the holding in the Pennsylvania case on which the Third Circuit rely is that clear or not that clear. Well, I certainly think it's not that clear. But if it were that clear, then you'd say, well, then the 11th Amendment would be no defense. It is possible to me that a judicial decision could be as clear as a statute. I certainly would concede that, but I would in no way concede that Joseph Smith is that clear. He went to an institution. Mr. Farr. Yes, Mr. Farr. Did the Court of Appeals make any finding that these officials had acted beyond the scope of their authority? They did not address the question at all in those terms, Justice Powell. Did the District Court make any finding in that respect? No, they did not. The District Court, in fact, to the extent they made any finding at all, indicated, although they found a violation of state law as such, indicated that the officials were acting in good faith and within the scope of their authority for purposes of giving them a qualified immunity on the damage plan. Is the Department of Public Welfare a party to this case? I've understood it was. Yes, I guess I believe it is. It's a state agency. It is a state agency. And it's the agency that oversees the operation of Pennhurst and other mental hospitals. That's correct. Now, the claim is certainly barred, I believe, against any state agency, in fact. Of course, what we're saying is that even though there are individual state officials named as well, the claim is barred with respect to them, too, because it is still a state agency. Well, the agency can operate only through officials and its other personnel. That's correct. Mr. Farr, what about actions of city or county officials under your hearing? The actions of the city and county officials are typically not subject to the same 11th Amendment analysis, but the situation you have here is that their activities essentially are to carry out the state law. The state provides all of the funding, and therefore, if the presumption is in effect and the new community facilities must be created and people must be moved into those facilities, the state bears 100 percent of the cost of that. And we think, therefore, in these circumstances, you can't get around that by simply naming the counties who have no fiscal responsibility separate from that of the state. Chief Justice, I'd like to save the remainder of my time for rebuttal. Very well. Mr. Rasha. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, even if the 11th Amendment prohibits a federal court decision on the state law issues in this case, principles of comedy do not. Rather, those principles prohibit federal courts as a matter of self-restraint from interfering with the operation of complex state programs, except when it's absolutely necessary to protect federal rights. Indeed, this Court has applied this rule to prevent the exercise of federal jurisdiction over federal claims when state forums were available to consider those claims. The rule is based in large part on principles of federalism, which require federal courts to respect the independence of local governments, state and county, in matters of local concern, especially when those matters involve the expenditure, as in this case, or the collection of monies. However, it is a rule which is also based on the very practical consideration that even the most simple and obvious principle of state law will involve incalculable legal and non-legal complexities in its application to ongoing state programs. Mr. Rasha, would you tell me when this issue was first brought into this case? It has been raised in various ways at various times in the litigation. It was raised in this form for the first time in the Third Circuit on remand when it was first suggested that the lower court order could be justified solely on state law. That was the first time when the respondents argued that the court should ignore the federal court issues and go directly to the state law issues. It was argued in the district court when the remedy was based on four federal theories and one state theory and then only in part on the state theory, as a limitation on the scope of relief, and again in the Third Circuit, on appeal from those four federal theories and one state finding, as a limitation on relief. But it was raised, and let me add to that, that we think it is the kind of issue that has to evolve during the course of the litigation depending upon the state of the litigation. And in this case, it is one that was raised in the form appropriate at every stage of the litigation. In this regard, as to the practical considerations, this court has recognized that federal courts are limited in their competence to decide the non-legal issues involved in operating state programs. Instead, it has required that federal courts give substantial deference to the professional judgments of state officials involved in operating those programs, even in cases involving constitutional issues where the federal courts can give a definitive and authoritative answer to the legal issues. When only state law is involved, federal courts are unable to even give that kind of a resolution of legal issues, and there is frankly just no justification for their involvement in the state decision-making process. For example, in this case, the lower courts have taken a vague right to treatment from a case in Ray Schmidt, in which Pennsylvania Supreme Court approved placement in an institution, and the lower courts created a presumption from that case in favor of placement in the community. As importantly, they took that right from a case involving one person, where funding was no issue whatsoever, and have created a presumption which applies, regardless of cost and available funding, to thousands of people. To say that that rule is less than definitive and less than authoritative is at the least a severe understatement. Nonetheless, in this case, acting to avoid, rather than to vindicate federal claims, the Third Circuit sanctioned a massive and ongoing intrusion into Pennsylvania's programs for the mentally retarded. In so doing, the Third Circuit, we believe, was deluded by the apparent simplicity of the right to treatment in the least restrictive environment, which we believed it had found in state law, and ignored the complexities of its application to even a single person, let alone the thousands of class members in this case. The extent of the resulting intrusion is fully reflected in the district court orders in this case. For example, under those orders, state and county officials are required to prepare and subsequently implement habilitation plans for every one of the class members. The manner in which those plans and programs are to be implemented, prepared, and monitored is strictly governed by the district court's latest 100-page order, which dictates the precise form such a plan shall take, the procedure by which it shall be prepared, who shall participate in its preparation, and how long it shall take to prepare it and subsequently to implement it. Was this order based on expert testimony of record? It was developed after the original trial based on testimony at record of the trial, I assume. It's never been quite exactly clear what its basis was at any given point in time. Are you suggesting the district judge just thought these things up on his own? There was various testimony at trial and in subsequent hearings as to how best to prepare habilitation programs and how best to implement them. I don't want to say he acted without a record. No, certainly there was a record created. I will say that he has taken it upon himself to control the matter in which state officials exercise or might exercise their discretion in this way. Does the record show the number of people in the class? At the time of trial, at the time of decision, there were over 1,100 people at Pennhurst and I believe several thousand more on the waiting list at Pennhurst, which was how the class was defined. By waiting list at Pennhurst, that means people who had applied for admission to Pennhurst and therefore had become eligible for other services in the community. They were all part of the class, and the class exceeded at least several thousand. But once again, I should note, and this is the next point I would make and perhaps best illustrates, the intrusive nature of the lower court's order and the broad gap between it and the judgment of state officials, and that is that it necessarily imposes upon thousands of other people who might be otherwise eligible for services in Pennsylvania, because the court has given absolute priority to its order over all other competing needs. It has on at least one occasion condemned state officials for moving residents out of another facility in Pennsylvania where conditions were clearly deteriorating badly, and this was a matter of record, where it was about to lose substantial funding, and said that that was unacceptable in light of his orders in Pennhurst, notwithstanding the fact that at that point Pennhurst, and today, was fully certified by the federal government as meeting minimum standards and was receiving substantial federal funding. The intrusive nature of the lower court's orders, it seems to me, is fairly obvious. State officials must conform their conduct to those orders, regardless of their own professional judgments and regardless of the legitimacy of competing demands for limited state resources. If they do not, they risk contempt, and in this case, that has been a very real risk. Less obvious are the invidious effects of the court proceedings themselves, regardless of the orders which are issued. Since the entry of judgment in 1978, there have been over 50 days of hearings held in the district court. There have been hundreds more before a hearing master appointed by the court to decide individual placement, make individual placement decisions. Each of these hearings must be attended by a state or county official, a professional who must spend time educating the judge so that the judge can make professional judgments or at least explaining and justifying their own judgments to the court or the hearing master. In either case, the effect is that limited and precious professional resources are wasted for the sole purpose of allowing a court and its master to substitute their own professional judgments for those of qualified state officials. This court has found this kind of judicial interference with professional decision makers to be unacceptable even in cases involving constitutional rights. When that interference involves the operation of a holy state program solely for the purpose of enforcing state law is a totally unacceptable exercise of the federal judicial power, and we suggest this court should stop it. Thank you, and if I may, I'd like to reserve the remainder of my time. Thank you. Mr. Gilhul. Chief Justice Berger, may it please the court. I will address jurisdiction, my colleague, Comedy. First, let me try briefly to put the case in perspective. This case went back to the circuit two and a half years ago in its eighth year, carrying the express instruction of this court to consider the state law issue in light of the recent state Supreme Court decision in Schmidt. The circuit and bank did so. In light of the state Supreme Court decision, all eight circuit justices unanimously ruled that state law is clear and that it was clearly violated, including Judge Alderser, who didn't like the state law, who would not have chosen it, who thought it unwise, but nonetheless clearly the state law. The state legislature sets state policy. The state legislative policy here, the preference for community facilities and the obligation to create them if they do not exist, arises from the state legislature and the state law. The circuit below, all eight justices, followed settled pendant jurisdiction principles, settled since Seiler and Green. That the 14th Amendment claims in this case are substantial, is undisputed here, and in light of this court's unanimous decision in Romeo, are indisputable. The same conditions, the same institution, Nicholas Romeo indeed a member of the class in this case. So far, there is nothing extraordinary about this case. What is extraordinary is petitioners' claim that principles of federalism, as they understand them, require a new 11th Amendment jurisprudence and a new pendant jurisdiction jurisprudence. But on the facts of this case, the result below serves both interests. The settled pendant jurisdiction doctrine is preserved, and federalism is served, since the state remains free to change its policy. Mr. Gillow, is it your position that the state officers here were acting without any authority, whatever, in the Larson and Treasure Selvore sense? Your Honor, I believe that is the necessary consequence of the circuit court's unanimous holding as to the clarity of state law. We argued the ultra-beerious argument last time, and I would rest upon that and upon this court's discussion earlier in colloquy with petitioners. Parsing that young-like fiction as to when it's state officers and when it's negligence and when it's outrageous is something of a judicial optical illusion. We would prefer, Your Honor, and it is the argument I will seek to make in a moment, to rest upon the real ground of young, which is the 14th Amendment pendant jurisdiction, 14th Amendment presence overcomes the 11th Amendment. Well, then, is it your position that you don't have to show here that the state officers were acting without any authority, whatever? Yes, Your Honor, we don't have to show that. How do you reconcile it with Treasure Selvore? Well, Treasure Selvore, Your Honor, was not a 14th Amendment case. This is. Why is this a 14th Amendment? Because I thought it turned on state law. No, Your Honor, it does not turn on state law, and that precisely is the number of the case. Here, the substantial 14th Amendment claim. Your Honor, if I may, may I step back from it just a moment? And I will return directly to your question. The settled principle of pennant jurisdiction is that once a federal court has jurisdiction by virtue of a federal question, it has it to decide the whole case, including the state issue, of which, if it stood alone, the state issue, it would not have jurisdiction. Now, it was Seiler which first applied this doctrine 70 years ago, precisely in the context of defendant state officials. Did it consider the 11th Amendment issue? Well, Your Honor, Seiler was decided a year and a week after Yon. It was decided in the midst of the storm of controversy. Is that a yes or a no answer? The answer is yes, Your Honor. It did consider the 11th Amendment? Yes, Your Honor. Ex parte Yon was argued to the Seiler court. That court, with the opinion written by Justice Peckham in Seiler as in Yon, could not have forgotten the 11th Amendment. To the contrary... Do you see, did Seiler consider the 11th Amendment argument in so many words? No, sir. It did not in so many words. I thought just a minute ago you answered me yes that it did. No, Your Honor. I answered yes. It did consider the 11th Amendment, Your Honor. And I say that because... Was it argued? Well, how can... Ex parte Yon was argued, Your Honor. Was the 11th Amendment mentioned by counsel in argument? Your Honor, I have not had access to the transcript of the argument. But the United States reports at that date summarize the argument. Yes, Your Honor, and the summary shows the mention of the 11th Amendment. Is there word in those summaries about the 11th Amendment? No, Your Honor, not the 11th Amendment. When was the last time Sala was cited in an 11th Amendment case? I'll make it easy. My recollection, Your Honor... I'll make it easy for you. Has it been cited since Lawson? Oh, yes, Your Honor. In what case? In my recollection, Your Honor... It was cited as an 11th Amendment case. Your Honor, my recollection is, and it may be in error, that it was cited in Edelman. In any event, it was cited that day in Hagen's. Not for your proposition that it was cited for the opposite. I think not, Your Honor. If I may spell out what it is my proposition is that I think Siler stands for. It is agreed, surely, that there was a substantial 14th Amendment question in Siler. May I ask you another question? What is the origin, the constitutional origin of the doctrine of pen of jurisdiction? Well, Your Honor, it is Osborne. It's what? It is Osborne. It's argument? Osborne, Your Honor. John Marshall's opinion for the court in Osborne. What is the constitutional provision on which it relies? Your Honor, it is derivative, is it not, of Article 3. Exactly. Exactly. And was the 11th Amendment adopted after Article 3? Yes, Your Honor, and it is Article 3, which it amends. It's quite specific, isn't it? Yes, sir. There's no question that the 11th Amendment is a jurisdictional provision. And is it not a general principle that a specific constitutional or statutory provision is to be favored over some general language that didn't mention the particular point at all? Yes. You would agree with that as a principle, wouldn't you? Yes, sir. I think that is so, though the decisions of this court, I believe, demonstrate the jurisdictional limitations of Article 3 to be even more sacrosanct than the jurisdictional limitations of the 11th Amendment. Which cases? Well, Your Honor, Seiler itself, and Young... Seiler didn't mention the 11th Amendment. Well, my point, Your Honor, is, as this court has held in many cases, that the Congress may overcome the jurisdictional limitations of the 11th Amendment as they may not those of Article 3. My point is that in many cases this court has held the jurisdictional limitations of the 11th Amendment may be waived. That is not so with respect to those of Article 3. And, of course, there is the Young Fiction with respect to the 11th Amendment and there is no such with respect to Article 3. Seiler articulated, and it itself is one of the significant early articulations of pendant jurisdiction, that such existed not only for the reasons articulated in Gibbs and its predecessors, namely the Article 3 jurisdiction over whole cases, the convenience, judicial economy, fairness to the parties considerations, but also to avoid premature and unnecessarily binding constitutional decisions and orders. Three years ago, in Mayer and Gagney, you unanimously held that a substantial 14th Amendment question, once in a case, remains in the case until the entire dispute is settled. There, there was a substantial 14th Amendment claim and the case had settled with injunctive relief on the pendant Social Security Act ground. The question was whether attorney's fees against state officials violated the 11th Amendment. In what the opinion of the court and the concurring opinion alike called the narrow ground, you held unanimously that respondent alleged substantial 14th Amendment claims resolves the 11th Amendment question. The same result, as I suggested that argument last time, obtains in Edelman. There, the court approved an injunction on pendant grounds, requiring state officials to timely decide public assistance claims. In Edelman, there was a 14th Amendment claim and pendant jurisdiction. The injunction rested upon the pendant federal statute under Hagen's. The pendant injunction here is and can be on no different jurisdictional basis from the pendant injunction in Edelman, for this court has never held that a spending power statute such as the Social Security Act in Edelman itself overrides the 11th Amendment. But you know, of course, that Edelman was a federal case, not a state law case. Your Honor, the pendant statute was a federal statute. The pendant statute here is a state statute. I think that makes no difference. I think the controlling matter is the presence of the 14th Amendment. Indeed, when petitioners argue, as they did again here, that the 11th Amendment would not bar relief if it had rested in a pendant federal statute, they are curiously incorrect. That is not so. Any old federal interest, no matter how significant, bar one, in any old federal statute, does not defeat the 11th Amendment and has never been held by this court to do so. Only Section 5, 14th Amendment statute do so. Are you saying the 14th Amendment issue remains in this case as it comes to us? And that was the unanimous holding of this court in Gagne v. Mayer. It remains in the case to the end and confers the jurisdiction and in light of Young and all that has followed provides the basis for affirmance below. What petitioners' arguments... So it's irrelevant, as you said earlier, I think, whether and to what extent these state officers are acting within their authority. You could reach the same result on that ground, Your Honor. But you say that as long as it's a pendant to a federal constitutional claim, that gets rid of the 11th Amendment right at the outset of the case. Yes, Your Honor, as I believe Edelman holds, as Gagne holds, and the same situation was presented in Hagen's, though again the 11th Amendment was not raised. But there again, this court, based on a substantial... the presence of a substantial 14th Amendment question, upheld injunctions based in pendant federal statutes which of themselves, a spending power statute, did not pierce the 14th Amendment.
